posts.content:
Originally on Facebook, 26 Feb 2011

Marriages are made in Heaven

Let’s admit it, marriages are made in heaven. But its purpose is to give men a taste of what to expect in hell. Any “man” alive with even an iota of belief in their heart would not dare question the above statement. Usually a man’s path to attain moksh is riddled with obstacles and all of them arising due to the opposite sex. Let me tell you a true story.

It was late at night when I came back from the office. The day has been long and I was tired. As I entered my apartment my mobile started ringing to wada raha sanam by abhijeet in a shrill voice (no sane man would set this as his ringtone. It was a demonic idea of my girlfriend and changing it would call for all hell to break loose.) Well it was an unknown number and I didn’t bother to pick up. As I changed and entered the washroom I heard my mobile ringing again. In the next 15 minutes it rang 15 times and I had to scurry in a wet towel to pick up the phone. I was irritated “Who is this?” A pleading voice from the other end replied, “dude its me” (it was a friend of mine who was in a serious relationship. I fail to understand if you are serious then why go in for a relationship and if you are in a relationship then you surely cannot be serious). What’s the matter bro, I inquired. “Help me dude, I am in Lake Police Station”. What? How did you manage to land up behind bars? “It’s a long story, just get me out of here”.

It was 12.30 when I reached the police station and bailed him out. It was a minor offence of drinking publicly and creating nuisance (read vomiting on the pavement). I put him in my car and drove back to my apartment. He started sobbing and no words would console him. It’s disgusting to watch a grown up man sobbing like a child. It’s even worse than watching a Tapas Paul flick if you know what I mean. Well I haven’t had my dinner and I guess he was also hungry after the ordeal. I started boiling some maggi on the oven. He kept on wetting my sofa in the drawing room.

It was past 2 in the morning when he sobered for a talk. “What happened bro?” I asked. This simple question opened the floodgate of rumbling words mixed with occasional bouts of sobbing and swearing. At the end of 2 hours and a couple of Saridon’s (for me) what I could stitch together was a sad story of a man being duped by a woman.

My friend gave GMAT and applied to IVY League Universities in the US and got final call from 3 places. His course was to commence from September. Everything was hunky dory until fate intervened. During his preparatory classes he grew close to a pretty lass. The girl got herself enrolled in an E grade management institute in Gobindopur (a god forsaken place and also the place of her ancestral home) and my numbskull friend to be with his love of life decided against going to US. But her father intervened in the affairs and got her engaged to a boy of his choice. And for the rest of the story you have to use your imagination.

After hearing his heart touching story I felt it to be my duty to get him out of this mess. In true sociopath manner the only thing to do now was to abduct……..it would be a quick seamless operation which would even put Toyota’s 6 sigma process to shame. We took the first train off to Gobindopur (obviously planes were not an option) and reached in the evening. We waited in a tea stall outside the station keeping a sharp eye on any approaching threat (my friend’s inlaws) and the night to become darker before we start our operation. Around 9 we came out off the shop and judged our way in the dark towards her house (my friend has visited her place only once before. We did not take any conveyance so that there is no evidence). It was pitch dark and was impossible to see the road. We have hoped for moonlight to guide us but we forgot to check the calendar. It was amavashya. The road was uneven and had potholes with little puddles of water. It was autumn and there was a chill in the air. Staying in the city we did not feel the chill but out here it made its presence felt. After walking for almost an hour we neared her house. There was a lot of light and decoration as if a celebration has been organized. But we could not hear any sound. We waited for a few more minutes outside, behind a bush carefully watching the proceedings. Around 10.30 the mosquito bites became unbearable and we decided to start our action. Slowly creeping over the boundary wall we entered the premise and proceeded towards her room. But suddenly there was a booming voice “who are you?” soon after we were surrounded by 20 burly men and by jove we were caught.

I would not go into the details of the humiliation that followed but suddenly there were excited shouts doing the round. “This was it”, I thought “the last I would breathe” and as we awaited our death trial some odd things started happening. We were carried to the lawn where a beautifully designed dias have been created. The next turn of events still gives me shivers at night. Even before we could say Ye Sali Zindgi we were married, my friend to his beloved and I to her sister. It seems the groom has backed out at the last moment citing more dowry. Just when the funeral songs were to be started two angels sent by god himself have arrived. Her parents were so obliged to see the angels they instantly announced a 1 ke saath 1 offer (I guess it was stock clearance, but what the hell….). The abducters were abducted and a poor soul in this play lost to the cruel plot of God.

Cut, Next Shot

My friend managed to join the December classes in one of the US Universities. The last I heard of him was that he has got a green card for permanent citizenship. It’s smart of him to stay back in US otherwise I would have skinned him raw, burnt him alive, thrashed his head………….but then I should not be complaining because I am a happily married man.

Om Shanti !!

posts.content:
Originally on Facebook, 25 Feb 2011

Love Guru Speaks

How to rescue a crumbling marriage?

On a spring morning while I was sipping a cup of fine blended Darjeeling tea suddenly there was a loud knock on my front door. As I opened the door I saw a scrawny man with a few days of unshaven beard nodding his head. Even before I could say something he briskly walked into my apartment and sat on my sofa and asked, “dude give me a cup of extra strong black coffee”. Where have I heard this voice? Then it dawned, its my friend who got married 6 months back. I haven’t seen him since then and “what has he turned himself into?” As I sat by him he gave me a weak smile and said “I know what you are wandering? Never get married dude, never, it would ruin your life.” It was awkward but I tried to sober him. Chillax dude ! Take a shower and let me make you a cup of tea and some breakfast. He looked at me with a vacant expression as I took his arm and walked him towards the washroom.

After a cold shower, clean shave and his tummy full as he sat in-front of me sipping the blended Darjeeling I saw colour return to his cheeks. Soon he started speaking about his terrible journey of life as a married man. I would not bore the readers with the intricate details of his tale because some of my married friends would already know and the others who are planning to get married might get offended. He stayed the whole day at my apartment, got exhausted narrating his sorrowful state, begged me to find a solution to his affairs and then slept. At night I took him to his house and deposited. While leaving I put a crumpled piece of paper in his hand and asked him to read it after I have left.

It’s been 2 months since and yesterday I got a call from him thanking profusely for my help and advice in bringing back his wife and love to his life. I was aghast. How could this have happened. My intentions were totally different. Let me explain what I wrote in that paper:-

Go for the trekking that you planned last year – My motive: get the hell out of your house and away from your wife. Instead both he and his wife started missing each other.Sell your car – My motive: this would impair his wife’s frequent visit to the inlaws’ house. It would also mean longer travelling time between office and home for him away from his wife. With this money my friend overhauled his furniture in his home and that too according to his wife’s preference. Redo your wardrobe – My motive: this would make his wife envious and suspect him of having an affair. Instead his wife was pleased that finally she was able to change his liking for clothes. Invest all your savings in a 20 year lock in fund – My motive: minimum disposable income for shopping. Well this also had an absolutely opposite impact. His wife took this as his sincere efforts toward securing their future. And finally start writing a blog and share everything you have in mind – I thought he would pour his frustration, angst and negative views of marriage in his posts. Also may be a few swear words against his wife. If all the above steps have failed this would have surely secured the guys life. Moreover this would warn any woman interested in him in the future to think against even speaking to him leave aside marrying him. But the almighty intervened and turned my cunning plot on its head. The idiot wrote how much he loves his wife, how he misses her and blah blah blah blah………..the asshole wrote 84 posts in 2 months. Man I have managed only 8 in the same timeframe. No wonder his juices have overflown in this short span (ahem ahem, no pun intended).

I feel like screaming, how the universe has conspired against my friend and his happiness. I see no hope left for his soul. Its time that I should take an active part in rescuing him from his marriage. I need to think, think deeply before its too late………….

P.S. Advices and comments are welcome. I hope you readers have understood the graveness of the situation. Be God with us.

AMEN !!

posts.content:
Originally on Facebook, 24 Feb 2011

Why people marry?

Is it for companionship, sex, money or love?

The other day one of my friends asked me “Dude I am confused. Can’t make up my mind why to marry?” My first thought was “don’t, it’s a sure way of slow poisoning yourself”. I could clearly see he was disturbed and this is not the advice he is looking for. I tried to make light of the situation and asked instead “have you thought of other alternatives” with a puckered smile. “Huh?” he was bewildered. I quickly managed the situation “have you spoken to your parents?” What followed as an answer was a painstaking narration of how his parents are hell bent on marrying him off to a pretty girl and their queer undertakings of convincing him to do the right thing. He then explained that he wants to concentrate on his career right now and have told his parents to back off. His parents have promised to tow his line but have insisted him on one last meeting later that day with a girl whose parents they have given words to.

The next day I happened to talk to another friend off mine from the fairer sex. I raised the same issue with her and was surprised to get a prompt and definitive answer with a snooty smile of a certain future Mrs. IIM – A. The conversation veered on dream of acquiring a host of tangible goods (posh flats, luxury cars, foreign escapades, unending shopping trips, etc, etc, etc) and intangible psychological one-up-man-ship over other girls about the derived pleasure of being Mrs. IIM – A. My next question was a blunder “what are you planning to give him instead?” Her voice suddenly sharpened “what do you mean? A life long commitment to love and care, what else would one want?” I could understand the unsaid words and the hidden threat “and if he tries to dishonour me I would wring his neck with my bare hands and drink his blood”......believe me it was scary. Her fiancé is doomed. I have touched a raw nerve of the opposite sex. The call ended soon after.

After ending the conversation with her I called my friend. His line was busy. I tried after 10 minutes, still it was busy. A sudden madness gripped me, I continued calling him after every 10 minutes but his number kept coming busy until it was 2 in the morning. I shouted on the phone WTF! Whom were you talking to? I have been trying to call you for the last 4 hours! I shouted a few more swear words. But I noticed a complete calm on the other side. I got nervous and thought “has my shouting burst his ear drums” or “has my swear words made him faint” (FYI….I have a repertoire of chosen swear words collected from blue blooded Jats in Delhi which can make even a rhinoceros bleed from its ears!). I was answered with a saintly voice as if coming from a distant land (or was it a network problem? any ways I was thinking of getting an Idea connection soon). I couldn’t catch the words at first. It was like a discourse on love by Baba Ondodev. “I am in heaven” he said. That explains the saintly calm, I thought…..”I am in love”. What? I blurted, "and I want to be with her for the rest of my life”,he continued……soon their was a rush of more Zen talks from him.

After half an hour I resigned and bid adieu to my friend. I had to clear off the super mush that has filled my head. As I lay on my bed blinking in the darkness thinking, my head swam and thoughts twirled and twisted to form a palette of white blinding light – a definite onset of Migraine. The guy has thrown his career plans and his life’s ambition in 1 single day and he now talks of marriage. Is this the same guy whom I considered the apostle of strength and a burning example of endearing the parental pressure against marriage. I lost all veneration for him.

Snap! An inner voice spoke “wake up dude. I have got the answer to the question why people marry”. Then I saw it :-

For women it is very simple:To derive a life long perverted pleasure of torturing another human being.

For men the answer may be summed up in either of the following two points:A momentary loss of sanity (I think this is what has happened to my friend)A natural instinct to take up challenges (and then fail miserably and curse the moment when the instinct overwhelmed every rational thought)

Alas as I sit writing this post I received an e-invitation for impending marriage from my friend. With a heavy heart I wish the poor soul all the luck and implore the almighty to bestow upon him the courage to withstand the oncoming disaster.

AMEN !!

The Federation International Philatelic (FIP) is extending its patronage, and the Federation of Inter-Asian Philately (FIAP) its auspices, for conduct of the Exhibition.

INDIPEX 2011, aims to bring the international philatelic community together to celebrate philately, and will provide a unique platform for interaction between all the philatelic stake-holders, viz. the collectors, the dealers, the philatelic journalists and publishers, the designers and security printers, and the postal administrations who issue stamps and stationery.

The exhibition will be largely competitive and showcase some of the finest and rarest stamp collections from around the world. Stamps reflect the history, culture, ethos and concerns of nations and people, which makes stamp collection as a hobby interesting and educative. By showcasing the best philatelic collections, INDIPEX 2011 looks to attract many newcomers to explore the fascinating world of philately.

There is considerable excitement about the exhibition all around the world as it will be one of the biggest events in India after the Commonwealth Games.

posts.content:
Originally on Facebook, 31 Oct 2010 · Reshared

Reading the annual Puja issues of a few Bengali magazines and came across this absolute gem of an article (in Anandalok) on the dialogues from Bengali potboilers (a large number of them starring Mithun), which have become popular in the last couple of years. It seems Mithun is doing to Bengali cinema today what he was doing to Hindi cinema in the mid-90s… adding commercial value with the touch of what is called B-grade masala!
I will not bother with a translation because nobody on earth can replicate the punch of a Mithun Chakraborty uttering… Hence, non-Bongs will have to excuse!
* In the bhog of Ma.
* Shaaper chhobol aar Cheetar khabol, jekhaney porbey arai kg manghso tuley nebey.
* Agnishwar Ray jekhaney paa rakhey, prothomey shey jaigata gorom hoi. Tarpor agun joley. Shesh hoi chhai diye.
* Marbo ekhaney, lash porbey shmoshaney.
* Fatakeshto khobor dekhena, khobor porena, khobor toiri korey. – both from MLA Fatakeshto (which is a Munnabhai look-alike, about a good-hearted goon becoming a MLA).
* Abhimanyu nag, jal-dhora noi. Jaat gokhro. Ek chhobolei chhobi.
* Public-er maar, Keoratala par.
* Nursery-tey shuru, half pantey guru, full pantey maha guru. (To try and give a context, this is from a film called Mahaguru!)
* Na ticket, na passport, shoja oporey.
* Shuru batam diye, interval-ey hospital, climax-ey chulli – Om shanti. (I never realised that a word like batam would find its way in a mainstream film!)
* Tor chhitkini-tey jong dhorey gechhey. Langcha shukiye bnodey hoye gechhey! (I am not sure of the context but is it REALLY about what I think it is?)
Thrilling!
What I found extremely irritating in the article was the supercilious tone of the author, who was trying to predict the downfall of the Bengali film industry due to the audience’s predilection for these ‘down market’ lines (while accepting that the films were huge successes purely on the basis of the dialogues).Happily, in the same issue, he also did an in-depth profile on Rakhi Sawant complete with details of her implants and ‘glamourous’ photographs. I hope he realized the wonderful irony!

posts.title: Boxers, Briefs and Books - John Grisham
posts.excerpt: I wasn’t always a lawyer or a novelist, and I’ve had my share of hard, dead end jobs. I earned my first steady paycheck watering rose bushes at a nursery for a dollar an hour. I was in my early teens, but the man who own…
posts.content:
Originally on Facebook, 24 Sep 2010

I wasn’t always a lawyer or a novelist, and I’ve had my share of hard, dead end jobs. I earned my first steady paycheck watering rose bushes at a nursery for a dollar an hour. I was in my early teens, but the man who owned the nursery saw potential, and he promoted me to his fence crew. For $1.50 an hour, I laboured like a grown man as we laid mile after mile of chain-link fence. There was no future in this, and I shall never mention it again in writing.
Then, during the summer of my 16th year, I found a job with a plumbing contractor. I crawled under houses, into the cramped darkness, with a shovel, to somehow find the buried pipes, to dig until I found the problem, then crawl back out and report what I had found. I vowed to get a desk job. I’ve never drawn inspiration from that miserable work, and I shall never mention it again in writing, either.
But a desk wasn’t in my immediate future. My father worked with heavy construction equipment, and through a friend of a friend of his, I got a job the next summer on a highway asphalt crew. This was July, when Mississippi is like a sauna. Add another 100 degrees for the fresh asphalt. I got a break when the operator of a Caterpillar bulldozer was fired; shown the finer points of handling this rather large machine, I contemplated a future in the cab, tons of growling machinery at my command, with the power to plow over anything. Then the operator was back, sober, repentant. I returned to the asphalt crew.
I was 17 years old that summer, and I learned a lot, most of which cannot be repeated in polite company. One Friday night I accompanied my new friends on the asphalt crew to a honky-tonk to celebrate the end of a hard week. When a fight broke out and I heard gunfire, I ran to the restroom, locked the door and crawled out a window. I stayed in the woods for an hour while the police hauled away rednecks. As I hitchhiked home, I realised I was not cut out for construction and got serious about college.
My career sputtered along until retail caught my attention; it was indoors, clean and air-conditioned. I applied for a job at a Sears store in a mall. The only opening was in men’s underwear. It was humiliating. I tried to quit, but I was given a raise. Evidently, the position was difficult to fill. I asked to be transferred to toys, then to appliances. My bosses said no and gave me another raise.
I became abrupt with customers. Sears has the nicest customers in the world, but I didn’t care. I was rude and surly and I was occasionally watched by spies hired by the company to pose as shoppers. One asked to try on a pair of boxers. I said no, that it was obvious they were much too small for his rather ample rear end. I handed him an extra-large pair. I got written up. I asked for lawn care. They said no, but this time they didn’t offer me a raise. I finally quit.
Halfway through college, and still drifting, I decided to become a high-powered tax lawyer. The plan was sailing along until I took my first course in tax law. I was stunned by its complexity and lunacy, and I barely passed the course.
Around the same time, I was involved in mock-trial classes. I enjoyed the courtroom. A new plan was hatched. I would return to my hometown, hang out my shingle and become a hotshot trial lawyer. Tax law was discarded overnight.
This was 1981; at the time there was no public-defender system in my county. I volunteered for all the indigent work I could get. It was the fastest way to trial, and I learned quickly.
When my law office started to struggle for lack of well-paying work — indigent cases are far from lucrative — I decided to go into yet another low-paying career: in 1983, I was elected to a House seat in the Mississippi State Legislature. The salary was $8,000, which was more than I made during my first year as a lawyer. Each year from January through March I was at the State Capitol in Jackson, wasting serious time, but also listening to great storytellers. I took a lot of notes, not knowing why but feeling that, someday, those tales would come in handy.
Like most small-town lawyers, I dreamed of the big case, and in 1984 it finally arrived. But this time, the case wasn’t mine. As usual, I was loitering around the courtroom, pretending to be busy. But what I was really doing was watching a trial involving a young girl who had been beaten and raped. Her testimony was gut-wrenching, graphic, heartbreaking and riveting. Every juror was crying. I remember staring at the defendant and wishing I had a gun. And like that, a story was born.
Writing was not a childhood dream of mine. I do not recall longing to write as a student. I wasn’t sure how to start. Over the following weeks I refined my plot outline and fleshed out my characters. One night I wrote “Chapter One” at the top of the first page of a legal pad; the novel, A Time to Kill, was finished three years later.
The book didn’t sell, and I stuck with my day job, defending criminals, preparing wills and deeds and contracts. Still, something about writing made me spend large hours of my free time at my desk.
I had never worked so hard in my life, nor imagined that writing could be such an effort. It was more difficult than laying asphalt, and at times more frustrating than selling underwear. But it paid off. Eventually, I was able to leave the law and quit politics. Writing’s still the most difficult job I’ve ever had — but it’s worth it.

The New York Times John Grisham is awaiting the release of his forthcoming novel The Confession

posts.content:
Originally on Facebook, 23 Sep 2010 · Reshared

A 15-volume 19th century compilation by British textile entrepreneur Thomas Wardle was hailed by experts and industry alike. Credit:IPS Correspondent
KOLKATA, India, Feb 4, 2010 (IPS) - A 15-volume documentation of 3,000 natural dyes by a 19th century British textile entrepreneur will be the focus of an upcoming international seminar on natural dyes in India.

On Feb. 20, a seminar dubbed ‘Raksa’ (Hindi word for ‘protection’) will be held at the Indian Council of Cultural Relations in Kolkata, capital of India’s eastern state West Bengal.

"The seminar is important for the revival of our indigenous handloom and dye industries, which offer livelihood to countless," said H.S. Debnath, the deputy director of the Botanical Survey of India (BSI), who discovered the omnibus. "Everything is now in the public domain and the industry can benefit."

Renowned natural dye experts Dominique Cardon of France, Brenda King and Jenny Balfour Paul of Britain are expected to attend the international gathering, said Debnath.

Unearthed from the dust that gathered for over 150 years in the BSI building in this eastern India metropolis, the find assumes significance for the sagging textile industry in India and the fashion world at a time when researches are looking for eco-friendly alternatives to chemical dyes. Debnath, by chance, found the volumes in a cupboard in his office in the old British-era BSI building in early 2009 in Kolkata.

The collection, ‘Specimens of Fabrics Dyed with Indian Dyes’, was compiled by 19th century textile entrepreneur Thomas Wardle (1831-1909) of Leek, a market town in the county of Staffordshire in Britain.

Wardle, who oversaw Leek’s growth as a power in the world of luxury textiles in the 19th century, was fascinated by India’s natural dye culture that he researched thoroughly the South Asian country’s ‘wild silks’.

Silk yarns and fabrics, which came from India and China, were dyed in Leek, using dyestuffs from all over the world. Around 1851 the British had taken all resources and the knowledge from South and Southeast Asia to revive the textile industry back home.

Debnath also found two other 18- and 14-volume companion tomes, ‘Textile Manufactures and Costumes of the People of India’ by John Forbes Watson, along with Wardle’s works.

Watson held the position of Reporter on the Products of India at the India Office in London, which was responsible for the direct administration of the former British colony in the 1850s.

The recently discovered volumes are considered so cardinal that the Feb. 20 seminar originally slated to be held in Paris has been shifted this month to Kolkata, once the capital of British India.

The discovery soon came to the attention of researchers like Cardon. "Renowned French archaeological textile expert Dominique Cardon, who is based in Paris, has already visited us. She is coming again for the seminar this month," said Debnath.

Cardon came to Kolkata to evaluate Wardle’s volumes on natural dyes, he said. She found Wardle’s document exceptional.

"People in modern times think that the traditional knowledge about herb- based dye is a secret. It’s not true. This document shows that," Cardon said in a meeting with the local media during her visit.

Debnath said researchers like Cardon were frantically looking for the works of Wardle. He said a few volumes of the works were available in London’s Victoria and Albert Museum, but the Kolkata discovery nearly completes the sets.

"We are excited and we hope UNESCO [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization] will recognise us. These 3,000 dye colours extracted from 64 plants can make 30,000 colours," said Debnath.

"Two more sets are missing and none knows where they are," said Debnath.

"We are lucky to have found this series. Else much of the indigenous knowledge gets lost," he said. "We have already started digitisation and conservation work of the volumes."

He said Wardle had pasted samples of each colour (like indigo, for which India is famous), numbered them and against each noted the recipes.

India’s environment ministry has taken interest in the discovery and has already sanctioned 50 million rupees (1.1 million U.S. dollars) for the preservation efforts. The country’s thousand-year-old tradition of natural dyeing has been applied to apparel, frescos and other articles.

"The saffron and maroon robes of the Buddhist monks, too, were dyed in vegetable colours," Debnath said.

The fashion and textile world was also excited to hear about the find. According to Kolkata fashion designer Soumitra Mandal, the volumes can open new horizons for the fashion industry, which has been exploring the use of eco-friendly materials and colours.

"I think it can lead to many things at a time when we are trying to move to eco-friendly outfits and shun use of chemicals," said Mandal, who has been designing outfits using ‘khadi’, the handspun cotton fabric popularised by the non-violent architect of India’s freedom movement, Mahatma Gandhi, as a symbol of protest against the British rule.

"With so much information typically lost over the years, it is a bit of a godsend for historians, technicians and textile lovers in general," said Rachel Bracken-Singh, owner of Anokhi, a chic textile firm in India’s tourist town Jaipur, which promotes hand-blocked prints, hand-woven fabrics and natural dyes.

"I am certainly very keen to see this expansive natural dye palette used in our textile past but largely lost in today’s modern textile world. From the perspective of learning about a more sensitive approach to the environment within the textile industry, this find is a real boon and very timely," she said.

According to Ashok Juneja, vice-president of The Textile Association (India), "This is definitely going to help the industry at a time when the emphasis is on natural and organic dyes. Things on those arenas are picking up."

S. Murugesan, chief of the Centre for Documentation, Research and Training on Natural Dyes at the rural welfare organisation Gandhigram Trust in south India’s Tamil Nadu state, said the discovery seemed very important.

"We are trying to commercialise the use of natural dye. But often we face the problem of viability and availability of raw materials. The series found in Kolkata can be of immense value," he said.

"India was one of the leaders in the knowledge and practice of natural dyes for textiles earlier with red, blue and yellow natural dyes in great demand. With the advent of the synthetic dyes, the knowledge and the practice of extracting and application of natural dyes were lost except in few communities in India," he said.

The Natural Dye Unit at Gandhigram, formed on the ideals of Mahatma Gandhi, is an effort to revive the knowledge of natural dyes among rural artisans and village textile workers. It also seeks to create an industry around the knowledge of natural dyes.

The unit, which started only with four dyes in 1987, today boasts an impressive 150 shades of natural dye colours completely standardised based on more than one raw material.

In Gandhigram these colours have been standardised for application in cotton, silk (about 100 shades) and woolen (40 shades). The unit concentrates on research, documentation and training in natural dyes besides production of natural dye-based cotton textiles.

According to Sunanda Mitra Roy, a researcher with the Kolkata-based Apparel Training and Design Centre (ATDC), synthetic dyes can cause skin cancer while natural dye is biodegradable and eco-friendly. "We can treat them, enhance the property and use (them) for commercial purpose," she said.

"If we can find cost-effective ways to use the knowledge, it can be useful. There is a need for awareness too," said Ranjan Dasgupta, joint director of ATDC. Natural Dye Omnibus Draws Top Researchers to India By IPS Correspondent

Originally on Facebook, 29 Aug 2010

Yada Yada Hi Dharmasya jotha jotha dharma
Glanir Bhavati Bharata glanimoy hobe ei bharat-e*
Abhyuthanam Adharmasya adhormer obhyuthan ghotbe
Tadatmanam Srijamyaham tatha tatha bivinno abotar rupe
Paritranaye Sadhu shishter poritran hetu
Vinashaya Cha Dushkrita dushkritir binashe
Dharma sangsthapunarthae ebong dhormo songsthapon-e
Sambavani Yuge Yuge ami jonmo nebo juge juge

The bengali translation is mine and not a copy pasted material. Hence a bit different from the contents available elsewhere.

* bharata have been translated in some places as "the descendent(s) of bharat", here reffered to Arjun, but I think its reffered to the place = bharat bhoomi or world and not to Arjun.
